title: How Topology Shapes the Phase Behavior of Polyelectrolytes
authors: David Beyer, Pierre J. Walker, Lena Tarrach, Zhen-Gang Wang, Christian Holm
abstract: We develop a topology-specific theory of polyelectrolyte coacervation using the random phase approximation and apply it to both simple and complex coacervation. Our results for stars and dendrimers show that more compact chain topologies display a greater propensity for liquid-liquid phase separation, as a function of both Bjerrum length and salt concentration. For mixtures of different topologies, we demonstrate that differences in polymer topology alone are sufficient to drive multiphase coacervation of polyelectrolytes, which we rationalize in terms of an effective $χ$ parameter. Analysis of a simplified global phase diagram reveals that the propensity for such topology-driven phase separation is largest at a finite molecular weight. Overall, our results establish polymer topology as a powerful design lever for tuning the phase diagram of charged macromolecules independently of molecular weight, net charge, and monomer chemistry, since changes in topology enable fine-tuning of the effective charge density without altering these molecular characteristics.
summary: This work establishes a theory showing that polymer topology dictates the phase behavior of polyelectrolytes, enabling control over coacervation independent of simple chemical changes. By using RPA within a statistical mechanics framework, the authors demonstrate that compact architectures enhance liquid-liquid phase separation propensity. This provides a powerful design principle for charged macromolecular systems.
main_problem: To develop a topology-specific theory for polyelectrolyte coacervation and understand how polymer architecture influences the phase behavior of charged macromolecules.
main_result: Polymer topology acts as a powerful design lever, allowing fine-tuning of phase separation propensity independently of molecular weight or net charge. More compact topologies exhibit a greater tendency for liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS).
method: The study employs a minimal theory combining the Flory-Huggins free energy with an electrostatic correlation term derived within the Random Phase Approximation (RPA).
model_or_system: The system consists of polyelectrolytes (charged macromolecules) forming simple or complex coacervates. Topologies studied include linear chains, stars, and dendrimers.
key_observables: Propensity for liquid-liquid phase separation (coacervation), effective $\chi$ parameter, charge–charge structure factor $S_{cc}(k)$, and salt partition coefficients.
important_parameters: Bjerrum length ($\lambda_B$), polymer topology parameters (e.g., number of arms $f$, generations $N_b$), molecular weight ($N$), and salt concentration.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Random Phase Approximation (RPA) for electrostatic interactions and assumes Gaussian chain statistics for structure factor derivations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate phase diagrams showing coexistence boundaries as a function of $\lambda_B$ or salt concentration, comparing different topologies. Other figures show salt partitioning behavior and scaling laws related to topology.
paper_structure: The paper develops the free energy functional using RPA, applies it to model various polymer topologies (linear, star, dendrimer), calculates phase diagrams for simple/complex coacervation under varying salt conditions, and analyzes the scaling dependence of effective interactions on molecular weight.
why_interesting: While focused on classical polyelectrolyte physics, the rigorous application of mean-field approximations (RPA) to complex many-body systems and the development of topology-dependent interaction parameters share conceptual links with modeling correlations in quantum many-body systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a): Polyelectrolyte solutions can split into a supernatant with a low polyelectrolyte concentration and a coacervate with a high polyelectrolyte concentration through LLPS. Blue and red chains correspond to polyanions and polycations, respectively. (b): Schematic representation of the different polymer topologies investigated in this work: linear chains, stars, and dendrimers. Note that for visual clarity, the different topologies are not shown at the same scale. (c): Overview of the different mixtures of polyelectrolytes studied in this work: simple coacervates (left panel), complex coacervates (middle panel), and salt-free, mixed complex coacervates (right panel).

FIG. 2. Phase diagrams of simple (subfigure (a) and (c)) and complex (subfigure (b) and (d)) coacervates of varying topology. Subfigures (a) and (b) show salt-free phase dia- grams as a function of the polymer volume fraction and the Bjerrum length. Subfigures (c) and (d) show diagrams in the presence of salt as a function of the polymer volume fraction and the salt volume fraction (the Bjerrum length is set to lB = b). Solid lines correspond to the co-existence bound- ary; dashed lines correspond to tie lines connecting coexist- ing phases (empty markers); solid markers denote the critical points.
